question: Pooled fund-total set and the fixed-cost-per-fund test: merge the 34 rule-F CFs from 990 narratives with the 15 web-sourced totals of b45n33-02-01 and the 4 Schedule A Part VI / Schedule D Part XIII totals (about 50 distinct CFs; Luzerne and NW Georgia overlap and agree), then run P-B45N33-02-01-04 (regress log opex on log total funds, log total assets and DAF share of funds)
conclusion_affected: Whether tail-CF operating cost is mainly a fixed cost per fund (rule F) or scales with assets (rule A); the rule-F tail cost figures
rationale: The 990 pass lifts n from 15 to 34 (38 with the extension), so the >= 40 threshold set in P-B45N33-02-01-04 is now reachable without new fetching. Per-CF F/A has median 1.13 and F > A at 24 of 34, so the per-fund signal is visible but not yet tested against size

question: Staleness of 'over N' totals: for the 17 tail CFs whose selected 990 total is a lower bound, compare the figure across FY2022-FY2024 returns (already cached) and against exact figures in adjacent years where they exist (e.g. Wayne County IN 382 / 396 / 394; Scranton 308 / 323 / 370), and estimate how far a repeated 'over N' understates the true count
conclusion_affected: Size of the upward bias in rule-F shares and costs for lower-bound totals (16 of 34 in the F set)
rationale: 16 of 34 rule-F totals (17 of the 36 CFs with a total) are 'over / more than / +' figures, which make share F and rule-F cost upper bounds. Dropping them moves the median share from 0.245 to 0.162, so the bias matters. The same narrative often repeats unchanged across years (Luzerne 'over 400' in FY2022-24)

question: Schedule D column (a) DAF count vs DAF assets at the smallest CFs: check the under-$1m CFs whose Schedule D DAF count is large relative to their DAF assets (Phelps County CF 38 DAFs at 0.5% of total assets; Polk County CF), reading the Schedule D Part XIII text and the DAF value per account, to see whether column (a) includes memorial, pass-through or zero-balance funds
conclusion_affected: Rule-F cost per DAF dollar in the under-$1m band (median 1,112 bps on n = 3 vs rule A 140 bps)
rationale: Rule F per DAF dollar explodes where many DAFs hold little money: Phelps County gives 10,073 bps under F against 140 bps under A. If column (a) counts dormant or pass-through accounts, both the DAF share of funds and the screened-account denominators are inflated

question: Run the same 990 narrative extractor (scripts/mission_fund_totals_from_990.py, Part III + Schedule O + Schedule A Part VI + Schedule D Part XIII) over the mid-size and large community foundations ($50m+ DAF assets) to compare the DAF share of funds and opex per fund with the tail
conclusion_affected: Whether DAFs are a larger share of funds at large CFs; the tail-vs-top cost-per-fund gap
rationale: Tail rule-F set: opex per fund median $4,398, DAFs 24.5% of funds. No comparable figure exists for larger CFs, so the tail cost-per-fund cannot be benchmarked. The extractor needs only cached or mirror XML (robots.txt 404 on the mirror)

question: Type-weighted rule F: where a full by-type fund list exists (990 sum-of-types: The Community Foundation for ... EIN 275098203, 136 funds; Loudoun 2022 report; Morton directory), weight funds by type using transaction intensity proxies (DAF grants per account vs designated / agency / scholarship payouts) and compare with equal-weight rule F
conclusion_affected: How far equal cost per fund misstates DAF cost when fund types differ in activity
rationale: Rule F assumes every fund costs the same. Its median share (0.245) sits between rule A (0.178) and rule G (0.356), consistent with DAFs being more active than the average fund. Only three tail CFs publish a complete type list, so this is a small-n calibration
